reference.source: U.S. Naval Air Station Patuxent River, 'Performance Test Each 1000th Airplane' (TED No. PTR-2125), 7 Sep 1944, F6F-5 BuNo 58310, Overload Fighter loading, military-power trial data as tabulated at wwiiaircraftperformance.org/f6f/f6f.html (summary table re-read 2026-09-12). That table states 'Gross weight -lbs 12,420' for this airplane, which is testMassKg = 5633.62 kg -- so the trial weight is stated and no substitution of a published normal-loaded weight was needed. topSpeedMps = 391.0 mph at an airplane critical altitude of 23,100 ft; climbRateMps = 2,660 ft/min at sea level. stallSpeedMps = 98.0 mph, the table's CLEAN, POWER-OFF stall: the flight model has no flaps or landing gear, so the clean figure is the like-for-like one. The same table's landing-condition power-off stall is 84.5 mph (37.77 m/s), which an earlier revision of this file cited by mistake -- it is unreachable for a model with no high-lift devices. Weights and dimensions cross-checked against the Grumman F6F Hellcat Wikipedia infobox (334 sq ft / 31.0 sq m wing, 42 ft 10 in / 13.06 m span, 9,238 lb / 4,190 kg empty). rollRateDegPerSec is NOT corroborated by this source and remains an unsourced estimate. takeoffDistanceM is the SAME table's 'Take-off distance, no wind' row: 755 ft = 230.124 m, FULL FLAPS, take-off speed 86.5 mph, 2700 RPM -- the table's other take-off figure, 335 ft in a 25-knot wind, is not used because the model carries no wind (Ruling R29). This is NOT a like-for-like figure: the model has no flaps (which pushes a simulated roll shorter than a full-flaps trial roll -- no flap drag to slow the acceleration) and no ground effect (which pushes it longer -- ground effect cuts induced drag and adds lift near the surface, both of which shorten a real roll, so a model missing it does not get that shortening). Plan 11a (2026-09-16) added rolling friction, which is now modelled and pushes the roll longer, moving the model from a -6.73% to a -0.605% under-estimate against the same trial figure. The take-off card grades this at a tolerance TIGHTENED, not widened, to 2% -- a characterisation lock on engine.staticThrustN, gear.rollingResistanceCoeff and reference.testMassKg rather than evidence of full flight-model fidelity, since flaps and ground effect still don't apply -- see tools/testcards/measure.ts and f6f.test.ts for the tolerance and the evidence it is built from. gear.travelSeconds and gear.dragAreaM2 are NOT corroborated by this source, or by NACA WR L-716 either: neither document times the gear cycle or gives a drag increment for it. Like rollRateDegPerSec above, both remain unsourced estimates -- 7 seconds is a round figure in line with the hydraulically-actuated retractable gear typical of WWII single-engine fighters of this class, and 0.3 sq m of drag area is a round, deliberately modest guess at the equivalent flat-plate area of two extended main legs, wheels and doors, well under the airplane's own zero-lift drag area of wingAreaM2 * cd0 = 0.65 sq m. Both are placeholders for Mark to retune once the airplane can actually be flown with the gear down. gear.rollingResistanceCoeff (0.02) and gear.brakingResistanceCoeff (0.4) are likewise NOT corroborated by this source or by NACA WR L-716 -- neither document measures ground rolling friction -- and are round, generic figures for a pneumatic tire on a hard runway (unbraked rolling resistance in the low hundredths; brakes-locked friction in the range commonly cited for aircraft tires), not F6F-specific data. gear.tailUpSpeedMps (15) and gear.tailwheelYawRateDegPerSec (20) are the same kind of unsourced estimate: no trial in this source times when the tail comes unstuck or how fast the tailwheel can swing the nose, so both are round, plausible placeholders -- tailUpSpeedMps well below the 38.67 m/s (86.5 mph) full-flap take-off speed the same table reports, and tailwheelYawRateDegPerSec picked independently of rates.maxYawRateDegPerSec's 15 deg/s of airborne rudder authority -- ground steering and airborne rudder are different mechanisms, so no relationship between the two numbers should be read into either value. All four are placeholders for Mark to retune once the airplane can actually be taxied. windmillCd0 = 0.0422 is an ENGINEERING ESTIMATE, not a trial figure, and is labeled as one here for the same reason rollRateDegPerSec is: no wind-tunnel or flight-test figure for a windmilling R-2800 disc on this airframe was located. It is 2.00x the clean cd0 of 0.0211 -- a windmilling constant-speed propeller roughly doubles clean parasitic drag -- taken as the MIDDLE of the published 1x-3x range for a stopped or windmilling propeller, which spans that much depending on blade pitch. Measured on this airplane 2026-09-16, level at 50 ft with altitude pinned so drag is the only loss, 250 mph bleeding to 100 mph: 79.3 s / 6.01 km with no propeller drag at all (the state Mark flew and reported as unrealistic), 50.5 s at 1x, 37.5 s / 2.70 km at this value, 30.0 s at 3x. Expect to tune it once someone flies a dead-stick approach. gear.heightM = 2.2 is an ESTIMATE, the same status rollRateDegPerSec above carries, not a trial figure -- neither this table nor NACA WR L-716 gives a static ground clearance or thrust-line height for the type. Derived 2026-09-16 (Task 15) from the real F6F-5's 13 ft 1 in (3.99 m) propeller and a three-point ground attitude leaving roughly 9 in (0.23 m) of tip clearance, which puts the thrust line about 2.2 m above the ground. Cross-checked against this project's own low-poly mesh (src/render/scene/hellcat.ts): its 3.9 m propeller disc, centred on the thrust line, reaches -1.95 m from the body origin, and 2.2 m clears that by 0.25 m -- enough that the disc, the 1.5 m fuselage box and the wing (thinnest point -0.39 m) are all comfortably above a runway placed at this height, without the margin being so generous that it stops looking like a taildragger sitting on its gear. The same table's landing-condition power-off stall is 84.5 mph = 37.7749 m/s and is now carried as reference.stallSpeedFlapMps and graded with the flaps set (Plan 11b, 2026-09-17) -- the note earlier in this string recording it as unreachable was true only while the model had no high-lift devices. flap.clIncrement = 0.4831 is DERIVED from those two stall speeds rather than estimated: stall speed goes as 1/sqrt(CLmax) at fixed weight, so (43.81/37.7749)^2 = 1.3451 is the CLmax ratio full flaps must produce, the shipped lift curve peaks at 1.400013 (measured 2026-09-17 at +15.5 deg, which is NOT aero.clMax -- that field is inert, see flap.clIncrement's schema comment), and 1.400013 * 1.3451 - 1.400013 = 0.4831 is the increment on clAtZeroAlpha that reaches it. flap.travelSeconds = 5 and flap.dragAreaM2 = 0.6 are NOT corroborated by this source and are estimates of the same status as gear.travelSeconds and gear.dragAreaM2: 5 s is a round figure for a hydraulic flap cycle on a fighter of this class, and 0.6 sq m is twice the extended gear's drag area, full flaps being the draggier device. dragAreaM2 is additionally expected to be CHARACTERISED by the take-off card, which grades against this table's own FULL-FLAPS 755 ft figure: with the flap lift increment derived and ground effect carrying no fitted parameter, flap drag area is the only unknown entering that measurement, exactly the role gear.rollingResistanceCoeff already plays. Read that agreement as a characterisation lock, not as evidence of flap fidelity. RE-MEASURED 2026-09-17 with flaps and ground effect both modelled, which makes the take-off card LIKE-FOR-LIKE against this table's full-flaps 755 ft run for the first time: the model reads 236.085 m at full flaps against 230.124 m, +2.590%, and the card's tolerance was re-measured from 2% to 4% accordingly -- the re-measure Plan 11a pre-authorised when it wrote that 11b's flaps were expected to move this figure and not to be chased back to it. flap.dragAreaM2 was deliberately NOT tuned to close that gap: fitting one free parameter to one trial number would make the card tautological, so 0.6 sq m stands on its independent grounds (twice the extended gear's drag area, and 92% of the airframe's own 0.655 sq m zero-lift drag area). The residual runs LONG for a named reason: the model has ground effect's induced-drag reduction but not its lift increase, and the missing lift would take weight off the wheels and shorten a real roll, so a model without it over-charges rolling friction for the whole roll. Expect this figure to move again if anyone adds ground-effect lift. gear.lateralGripSeconds = 1.5 is an ESTIMATE of the same status as the other gear figures -- no trial in this source measures how quickly a tire kills sideways motion. It is a placeholder for Mark to retune once he has flown roll-outs, and it is a time constant rather than a hard constraint so that a mishandled touchdown can still swap ends: 11a measured a taxi turn reaching 113.6 degrees of sideslip with no lateral force at all, which is the behaviour it replaces. aero.cySlopePerRad = 2.00 is MARK'S ARCADE NUMBER, deliberately TWICE the top of the published range (Cy_beta for this class runs about 0.5 to 1.0 per radian referenced to wing area). History, all 2026-09-17: shipped at 0.10, a ninth of where it belonged; raised to 0.90 once the two harness defects that had pinned it were gone; Mark flew 0.90, liked the lateral movement, asked for 1.0 (retention 74%); then asked for the rebound to be cut so ~90% of a new heading survives a rudder release, and chose 2.0 from a measured grid of this coefficient x rates.weathercockSeconds (retention 88%: 16.7 deg held, 14.7 kept; slip while held 6.3 deg). Later that day rate authority became proportional to speed instead of dynamic pressure (rateAuthority in src/sim/flight/model.ts -- Mark's decision, made to fix roll response at approach speed, accepting that it re-tunes the rudder); at 50 m/s the rudder and fin rates roughly doubled and retention re-measured at 85% (26.5 deg held, 22.4 kept), sustained rudder for 30 s giving heading 163.1 / track 153.2 / slip -9.8. The trade he accepted, measured on that grid: full rudder at 200 m/s now pulls about 4.8 g sideways and turns flat at 8.4 deg/s against 4.9 deg/s for a 60 deg bank (at 50 m/s it is 0.23 g and 4.6 deg/s against 19.5 banked, so this is a high-speed effect only). A lateral-g cap on sideForceN was offered alongside and NOT applied -- he asked for the coefficient alone. Physically the rebound IS the sideslip realigning, and a real rudder-only turn retains little (what turns a real airplane on rudder is the roll it induces, which this model does not have), so 88% is an arcade choice made knowingly. The metric it was chosen by is heading RETENTION, which is what Mark's complaint was about: hold 5 s of full rudder at 50 m/s, release, fly 15 s hands-off, and see how much heading survives the weathercock returning the nose to the relative wind. Measured 2026-09-17: 0.10 held 14.3 deg and kept 4.1 (29%), and he reported the rudder as completely inadequate at it; 0.50 kept 57%; 0.90 held 15.5 deg and kept 11.1 (72%). NOT measured by lateral displacement: 3 s of full rudder moves the airplane under a metre at any of these values, bank is the right way to translate, and Mark agreed he is not asking the rudder to do that. The two harness defects, both pre-existing and both exposed by this term rather than caused by it: the altitude-hold assist's departure test, resolved by deleting that assist at Mark's request; and measureClimbRate in tools/testcards/measure.ts, first diagnosed as PATH-DEPENDENT (a fast and a slow settling branch at the best-rate attitude) -- which it was NOT. Re-measured: every attitude from 0 to 30 deg settles to one wings-level, zero-sideslip state and reads 15.775 m/s identically at every coefficient; the non-monotonic pass/fail (0.2 fails, 0.5 passes, 0.7 fails, 0.9 fails) came from 32-40 deg sweep points that departed in the transient, were still tumbling when the 1 s sample window opened, happened to be unstalled throughout it, and read whatever the tumble was doing that second. Fixed the same day: the card now accepts only a STEADY sample (at the commanded attitude, wings level, no sideslip, unstalled, vertical speed steady -- bounds tabulated in measure.ts), and a new card in f6f.test.ts asserts the climb rate is bit-identical at 0.2, 0.5, 0.7 and 0.9. What raising it moved elsewhere, all re-measured and recorded in the tests concerned: the weathercock nose-swing from a 10 deg hands-off crab fell from 9.19 (0.10) to 6.08 (0.90) to 5.84 (1.00) to 4.16 deg (2.00) -- more of the slip is removed by the track bending, less by the nose -- with its floor now 3; its one-tau slip check stopped being a share-of-slip floor (that was asserting the side force stays weaker than the fin) and now asserts monotonic decay without overshoot; the frame-path auto-rudder wiring test re-recorded its arms (2.236 deg unassisted, 1.100 assisted, against 4.895 / 1.502 at 0.10); and the golden rolling-descent trajectory was regenerated at each step (it ends slower and higher, which is the sign an energy-removing lateral force must have). Added because the model had no lateral aerodynamic force at all: holding rudder built sideslip to the weathercock equilibrium of maxYawRateDegPerSec * weathercockSeconds = 22.5 deg and the heading then never changed, because nothing converted sideslip into a sideways push and the flight path never bent round to follow the nose (Mark, flying it 2026-09-17). Expect to retune it once someone has flown a few crosswind-style corrections on final. rates.altitudeHoldSeconds was removed on 2026-09-17 along with the altitude-hold assist itself: Mark asked what the feature was, established he had never requested it (it entered as the master spec's 'combat trim' and Plan 3 renamed it), and had already defaulted it OFF on 2026-09-15 for being unrealistic. Its departure test was what pinned aero.cySlopePerRad five times below the physical range, so deleting the feature is what let the rudder work.

combat.source: Six .50-cal guns: National Naval Aviation Museum https://www.history.navy.mil/content/history/museums/nnam/explore/collections/aircraft/f/f6f-5-hellcat.html . 800 rpm is a choice within the 750-850 rpm range and 883.92 m/s converts 2900 ft/s in the US Navy Aircrewman's Gunnery Manual https://www.ibiblio.org/hyperwar/USN/ref/AirGunnery/GUNS.html . 400 rounds/gun: Patriots Point Naval & Maritime Museum https://patriotspoint.org/things-to-do/aircraft/f6f-hellcat . Verified 2026-09-19. Convergence, dispersion, lifetime, drag, HP, per-hit damage, leak/decay rates, mounts and hit zones are gameplay ESTIMATES. Hitboxes approximate the existing procedural mesh, not a sourced installation drawing. No penetration model.

stores.source: Six HVARs, three under each wing; single bomb racks under each wing inboard of the undercarriage bays; 1,000 lb class per rack: English Wikipedia, 'Grumman F6F Hellcat', read 2026-09-20. HVAR: 134 lb (61 kg) all-up, 45.5 lb (20.6 kg) warhead, 1,375 ft/s (419 m/s) plus the speed of the launching aircraft: English Wikipedia, 'High Velocity Aircraft Rocket', read 2026-09-20; designation-systems.net 'Air-Launched 5-Inch Rockets' gives 64 kg / 20 kg / 5 km range. Burn time 1.0 s is an ESTIMATE: neither source states it. AN-M65 1,000 lb GP: 530 lb (240.9 kg) Amatol filler, 53% of total weight, so 1,000 lb (453.6 kg) all-up: Australian War Memorial C285409 and bulletpicker.com 'Bomb, 1000 lb GP, AN-M44, AN-M65, AN-M65A1', read 2026-09-20. dragAreaM2, dragPerM, damage, roundDamage, blastRadiusM, armS, lifetimeS are ESTIMATES or gameplay choices, in the same standing as combat's dispersion and HP figures. dragPerM for the bomb was chosen against an estimate of "about 1,200 m downrange and roughly 200 m/s" for a release at 120 m/s from 1,500 m; measured 2026-09-22 by tests/sim/strike.test.ts, which is where Plan 6b said the actual figure would be recorded, it is 17.67 s of fall, 2,066 m downrange and 202.9 m/s at the water. The speed estimate held; the range estimate did not, and this sentence carries the measurement instead of the guess.
